Macrons

Consonantal i

Theme

Money, work & business · Work & responsibility

wage noun

also wages, pay, daily wage, a day’s pay

classical

Sall. Cat. 37.7: manuum mercēde inopiam tolerāverat, had kept poverty off with the wages of their hands
Traupman 403: mercēdem accipere, to receive wages; mercēdem tribuere, to pay wages
M-O s.v. salary, pay (of employees), wages

mercēs, mercēdis f.

noun, third declension

pay, wages (for work done)

What any work earns: a labourer’s wages, a teacher’s fee, an actor’s pay; also rent (see rent, money paid for a house or flat). A day’s wage is mercēs diurna: mercēde diurnā conductum, a man hired by the day (Hor. S. 2.7.18).

Examples

  • ingrāta es, inquit, ōre quae nostrō caput incolume abstulerīs et mercēdem postulēs

    ‘Ungrateful creature,’ he said, ‘you got your head out of my mouth unharmed, and now you want paying?’Phaedr. 1.8.11–12

  • dignus enim est operārius mercēde suā

    for the labourer deserves his wagesVulg. Lc. 10.7

Other words

  • mercēdula, mercēdulae f. — small wages, poor pay

    noun, first declension · also used · classical · Cic. de Or. 1.198: īnfimī hominēs mercēdulā adductī, the lowest of men, drawn by a little pay

See also salary, earn, employee, employer, rate, income.

SourcesLewis & Short: merces · Lewis & Short: mercedula
